title: Continuation of the National Emergency With Respect to Iran
summary:
The White House has renewed the national emergency related to Iran for another year. First put in place in 1979, this policy stays in effect because relations with Iran have not normalized and work tied to agreements from 1981 is still ongoing.

In practice, this renewal keeps existing measures and authorities in place that the U.S. uses to address security, foreign policy, and economic concerns linked to Iran. The notice also makes clear that this decision is separate from a different Iran-related emergency first declared in 1995 and renewed earlier this year.

Who benefits? U.S. policymakers and agencies keep the legal tools they rely on to manage risks and maintain pressure on Iran. Partners that align with U.S. policy may welcome the continuity. People and institutions involved in long-running claims and agreements dating back to the early 1980s may also see continued clarity while those processes move forward. For businesses, consistent rules—even restrictive ones—can reduce uncertainty about what is and isn’t allowed.

Who may be negatively affected? Iranian state-linked entities and sectors already facing U.S. restrictions will continue to encounter limits on access to U.S. markets and finance. U.S. and foreign companies interested in new trade or investment with Iran will likely remain on the sidelines. Banks and global payment networks will keep bearing compliance costs. Some humanitarian and people-to-people efforts could be slowed by risk concerns and paperwork, even when exemptions exist.

The notice will be published in the Federal Register and sent to Congress as part of the regular process.
